items.titel: Cristina Fernández Cubas wins 2026 Cervantes Prize for Spanish literature
items.anriss: The Catalan writer, a leading figure in the short story and fantastic literature, becomes the seventh woman to receive the top Spanish-language literary award.

absaetze.t: Published on 3 November 2026 - 22:17 GMT+1
The Catalan writer Cristina Fernández Cubas was on Tuesday named the winner of the Cervantes Prize 2026, the highest distinction in Spanish-language literature, worth 125,000 euros.
ADVERTISEMENT
The Minister of Culture, Ernest Urtasun, announced the jury's decision, which acknowledges her contribution to renewing the contemporary short story.

The jury highlighted "the originality, excellence and coherence" of a body of work that has transformed Spanish-language fantasy fiction. It also praised her ability to explore human experience through stories marked by mystery and ambiguity.

Born in Arenys de Mar (Barcelona) in 1945, Fernández Cubas is one of the leading figures in Spanish short fiction. Among her works are 'Mi hermana Elba', 'El ángulo del horror' and 'La habitación de Nona'.
Over the course of her career she has also received the National Narrative Prize and the National Prize for Spanish Literature.

With this recognition, Fernández Cubas becomes the seventh woman to receive the Cervantes, following in the footsteps of writers such as María Zambrano, Ana María Matute and Elena Poniatowska. The prize consolidates her career and her influence on new generations of writers.

items.titel: EXCLUSIVE: SNC pulls out of Navy’s trainer jet competition
items.anriss: The service is now planning to issue an award for the UJTS program between July and the end of September 2027.

absaetze.t: PARIS — Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) is no longer competing for the Navy’s new training jet, Breaking Defense has learned, leaving the service with one true competitor: Textron Aviation Defense with its M-346N trainer.

“With great respect for the Navy and PMA-273, SNC could not responsibly bid the UJTS [Undergraduate Jet Training System] program under the current contract structure,” SNC said in a statement to Breaking Defense today in response to questions about whether it formally bid on the program by the Oct. 30 deadline. “We do remain committed to naval jet training and stand ready to re-engage if the approach is revisited.”

Textron Aviation Defense, the only known major competitor to SNC, confirmed to Breaking Defense that the firm submitted its offering of the M-346N to the Navy. Barring a reopening of the competition or a surprise entrant, it appears the de facto winner will be the M-346N.
A spokesperson for Textron told Breaking Defense in an email today that the firm is “ready to support the U.S. Navy and its future training needs.”

The field of competitors for the UJTS program had already narrowed in recent months, after Lockheed Martin announced in April it would not submit its offer of the TF-50N with Korea Aerospace Industries for the program. Similarly, Boeing announced in June it also would no longer participate in the competition. Then in September, Breaking Defense reported that Northrop Grumman was dropping off SNC’s bid, which was based around a clean-sheet design known as the Freedom. (Stavatti Aerospace, a group that regularly claims to have aerospace designs for every Pentagon contract, said on Oct. 30 that it submitted a bid on UJTS.)

The Navy plans for the UJTS to succeed the service’s T-45 Goshawk fleet that first entered the Navy’s fleet in the early 1990s to train both Navy and Marine Corps aviators for jet carrier aviation and tactical strike missions. The program office for UJTS told Breaking Defense today that the service stuck to an Oct. 30 deadline for requests for proposals for the program from industry — itself an extension from a previous RFP deadline of June 30.
The service also revealed it is slightly pushing back the timeline for awarding a contract on the closely-watched program.

While the Navy last said in a September request for proposal (RFP) that it planned to award a contract for the program by June 2027, the service is now estimating it won’t do so until sometime between July and the end of September 2027. That’s not the first time the award date has been pushed back, and the service originally planned to make a selection in March 2027.
“The Government is in source selection with the intent to award the UJTS procurement in 4QFY27,” the office said.

While the T-45 lands on aircraft carriers, the Navy shared in a March RFP that it won’t require the new trainer jet to do so. The Navy also said it isn’t requiring the new aircraft to support field carrier landing practice (FCLP) to touch down, which seeks to simulate a carrier landing on an airfield runway.
Rather, the aircraft must support FCLP to wave off, and the Navy said in the notice that industry should share “unique aircraft simulation capabilities” to train aviators for carrier landings.
UPDATED 7:10 p.m. EST: This story has been updated with comment from Textron Aviation Defense.

items.titel: What Trump’s Drastic Reduction Of U.S. Military Aid To Israel Could Mean
items.anriss: By the end of the year, the U.S. will stop providing Israel with billions of dollars in annual assistance, President Donald Trump proclaimed Tuesday morning . The announcement was delivered as both Washington and Jerusalem are mulling …

absaetze.t: By the end of the year, the U.S. will stop providing Israel with billions of dollars in annual assistance, President Donald Trump proclaimed Tuesday morning. The announcement was delivered as both Washington and Jerusalem are mulling plans for a new wave of attacks on Iran and amid increasing American voter antipathy toward the Israel in the wake of the Gaza war and America’s involvement in the war with Iran.

While Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin “Bibi” Netanyahu has openly discussed weaning his country off direct U.S. assistance in favor of more cooperation on weapons development, the Trump announcement still caught many there by surprise. It also raises a lot of questions about Congressional authorization and the impact on future sales of advanced arms from U.S. manufacturers, many of which are planned, that still have to be answered.

“As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that – we give Israel $4 billion a year – and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” Trump told Fox & Friends Tuesday morning during his message to American voters going to the polls for the midterm election. “And they’re fine with it because you know they have become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying anymore to Israel, so it’s just a wasted thing because we’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel.”
“Now we’ll help Israel if they need it,” the American leader added. “You know they’ve been a great ally, and we’ve been the greatest of all allies to many many countries.”

Trump did not elaborate on what specific expenditures he was referring to, and we’ve reached out to the White House for more details. However, the president was almost certainly talking about the ongoing decade-long Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Israel.

The MoU calls for providing $3.8 billion in annual aid and it is drawing to a close. Set to run through 2028, the vast majority of that funding is for Foreign Military Financing (FMF) to purchase weaponry mostly from American manufacturers.

“In 2016, the U.S. and Israeli governments signed their third 10-year Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on military aid, covering [Fiscal Year] 2019 to [Fiscal Year] 2028,” according to a 2025 Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. “Under the terms of the MOU, the United States pledged to provide—subject to congressional appropriation—$38 billion in military aid ($33 billion in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) grants plus $5 billion in missile defense appropriations) to Israel.”
The MoU is merely a promise and not legally binding. Congress has to approve any funding requests.
A New Deal
Washington and Jerusalem began negotiating a new MoU in June, according to the Israeli Defense Ministry (MoD).

“The new framework, reflecting the strategic vision of Israel’s Prime Minister and Minister of Defense, is designed to strengthen the IDF’s qualitative military edge through expanded joint investment in research, development, and co-production, deepen the U.S.-Israel partnership demonstrated during Operation Roaring Lion, and gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership,” MoD explained.
Netanyahu has been warning Israel for months that it would have to face reduced assistance from the U.S.

“If you think we will continue receiving what I secured twice — tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget — you’d better prepare yourselves and get used to the idea that this will not continue,” he told Israeli media last month, according to Bloomberg News. “That is because America has changed, not because Israel has changed. It will end. It is only a matter of time.”
Netanyahu added that Israel has two more years with Trump, but must prepare for a less favorable Washington after he leaves power.

In January, the Israeli leader said he wanted to reduce Israel’s reliance on American aid. He told The Economist that he was not seeking the full renewal of the MoU, which has to be renegotiated by 2028.
“I want to taper off the military aid within the next 10 years,” Netanyahu told the publication. Asked if he meant “to taper it off to zero,” Netanyahu said “yes.”

“We want to be as independent as possible,” the Israeli leader proffered. Referring to his meeting with the the American president in Florida in late December, Netanyahu added: “In my visit to President Trump, I said we very deeply appreciate the military aid that America has given us over the years, but here too we’ve come of age, and we’ve developed incredible capacities.”

For Israel, the MoU “now matters less for the money it provides than for what it signifies: a gauge of the depth and durability of U.S. support,” the Crisis Group think tank argued in August. “To be sure, FMF has enabled Israel to build up its military power without fully bearing the cost, and phasing out this assistance would impose real burdens. Israel would have to pay for critical U.S. weapons from its own budget.”

However, with its annual GDP now exceeding $700 billion and defense spending above $40 billion, “Israel has found increasing difficulty in arguing that it requires an additional $3.3 billion each year for military purchases,” Crisis Group posited. “Netanyahu has asked the finance ministry to allocate billions of dollars in additional funding for the defense budget over the next decade, a large portion of which would be earmarked to procure U.S. fighter jets, on the assumption that Israel will no longer receive the funds necessary for these purchases from Washington.”

Since the attack by Hamas, U.S. money from the MoU has made up a smaller percentage of the Israeli MoD’s overall budget as the country has increased its own defense spending. Those funds have also been bolstered by several large tranches of U.S. supplemental aid to procure bombs and other weapons.

“For most of the last 15 years, the $3.3 billion Israel receives annually in FMF made up roughly 20% of Israel’s defense budget, which was itself 5-6% of Israel’s GDP in the same period,” the Israel Policy Forum (IPF) explained in May. “Both Israeli defense spending and the share coming from U.S. aid slowly declined amid major economic growth throughout the 2010s, and then spiked in 2023 following the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel and ensuing wars.”

IPF stated that after the Hamas incursion, “Israel sharply increased defense spending (both within the regular budget framework and in extraordinary expenditures) to 8-9% of GDP, and the U.S. gave Israel several large supplemental security assistance packages between late 2023 and early 2026 in addition to the MOU-directed security aid.”

“The net result, taking into account both much higher Israeli spending and large amounts of American aid, is that in 2024 U.S. assistance briefly accounted for more than one third of Israel’s defense budget,” IPF noted. “In 2025 this figure dropped to close to 10%, with Israel spending an estimated NIS 168 billion ($52 billion) on defense in that year.”

Until recently, “Israel had been given a partial exemption” on the requirement that FMF funds be allocated for American products,” the Crisis Group noted. This allowed Israel to “invest a portion of the money in its own defense industry, Crisis Group explained. “This carveout, in turn, has made Israeli firms more competitive in the arms export market.”
Heavy Reliance On American Hardware

Israel, which has received more than $175 billion in U.S. aid since its creation in 1948, relies heavily on American weaponry. The Israeli Air Force (IAF) tactical aviation fleet consists of U.S.-built F-15s, F-16s, F-35s and AH-64 Apache attack helicopters, among other U.S. types. Israel also made deals for a number of other platforms including KC-46A aerial refueling tankers and CH-53K heavy-lift helicopters and it uses large amounts of American precision munitions. Meanwhile, Israeli missile defense systems like Iron Dome and Arrow 3 have been developed with significant assistance from the U.S.

A top Israeli MoD official told The Times of Israel (ToI) last month that his country wants to flip the switch to add value to the American defense industry by using its experience developing weapons as it fights seemingly constant wars. The continual threats from regional actors and terror groups allow Israel to serve as a testing ground for U.S. defense technologies, Aviram Hasson, director of the Defense Ministry’s mission to the US and Canada, explained.

“Hasson pointed to engineering breakthroughs and intellectual property emerging through development of Israel’s active-defense systems, saying every US government request for technology arising from the long-range anti-ballistic missile Arrow 3 program has been fulfilled,” the publication noted.
“It is clear on both sides of the ocean that this cooperation is a strategic need of both powers, not only of Israel,” Hasson told ToI.
U.S. Has Paid Far More Than $4B A Year For Israel’s Defense

Beyond direct financial aid, the U.S. has expended a great deal of resources defending Israel over the past several years. This has included defending against multiple Iranian missile barrages on Israel on top of participating directly in two wars. In addition, there were the constant drone and missile battles in the Red Sea with the Houthis, who began attacking shipping there in response to Israel’s war in Gaza. Part of the U.S. operation against the Houthis was also providing a layer of protection against long-range missile and drone launches at Israel by the rebel group.

During the course of all these events, the U.S. deployed a very large number of its available warships, aircraft, and air defenses, as well as thousands of personnel, to the Middle East at great expense, both in dollars and the toll on troops and equipment.

Just this year alone, 23 U.S. troops have died and nearly 900 have been injured since the launch of Epic Fury in February. Dozens of aircraft have been destroyed and U.S. bases in the region have been partially destroyed and will take billions to repair.
The U.S. has also fired off a large amount of its own munitions defending Israel from attacks by Iran and its proxies. This has contributed heavily to shortfalls in America’s own stockpiles.

All told, the U.S. has spent nearly $50 billion just on the most current conflict with Iran, far exceeding the $4 billion Israel gets per year in annual direct aid. Then there is the opportunity cost of the massive wear and tear on the force and the U.S. military’s overall capacity to fight in the near and medium term due to all these engagements.

All that being said, it can be argued that the U.S. had major interests in participating in these conflicts beyond just the defense of Israel. It is rarely just that simple. The Iran nuclear program, for instance, has impacts much farther than the Middle East and Israel. Still, the U.S. has poured unprecedented resources into Israel’s defense and these investments far eclipse the $4B being discussed today.
Surprise In Israel
Many Israeli government officials were caught completely off guard by the Trump announcement, according to Politico.
“Officials in the Finance Ministry say they were surprised by U.S. President Donald Trump’s announcement that military aid to Israel would cease by the end of the year, ” the publication reported.

“No formal document was submitted from the Prime Minister’s Office regarding the end of aid,” Politico added. “The ministry was aware of the intention to end it, but was surprised by the intention to do so immediately.”
Officials in the Defense Ministry and the military were also reportedly surprised by the announcement, according to the Post.
“We did not expect this announcement, certainly not today,” a senior defense official told Israeli media.

“There is ongoing dialogue with the Americans, and we can say that we were surprised. We will study the implications of the decision, which has yet to reach professional officials,” the official is quoted as saying.

items.titel: Exhibition as Living Archive: the 1950s Baghdad Modern Art Group in the UAE Today
items.anriss: The Baghdad Modern Art Group was established in 1951 by two of Iraq’s most influential artists, Jewad Selim (1919–1961) and Shakir Hassan Al Said (1925–2004), and grew to engage many of Iraq’s leading artists, architects, poets, and more. …

absaetze.t: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group, Curated by Nada Shabout, on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027
November 3, 2026 — 3 min read

The Baghdad Modern Art Group was established in 1951 by two of Iraq’s most influential artists, Jewad Selim (1919–1961) and Shakir Hassan Al Said (1925–2004), and grew to engage many of Iraq’s leading artists, architects, poets, and more. Together, they sought to develop a new art form, one that negotiated a time of globally inflected modernism from Baghdad, an Abbasid city (est. 762 CE) that traces its lineage to the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia. In All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Dr. Nada Shabout brings together the artists from this circle, as well as those whom its work influenced, both at the time and in the following generations, until today.

After the Kingdom of Iraq’s formation in 1932 as an independent state, Iraqi artists explored the new parameters of the secularized, modern society that was emerging following Britain’s maneuvering to dismantle the Ottoman Empire. Artists questioned the ability of traditional “Islamic art” practices to present their contemporary realities, searching for a more effective visual language. In this context, modern art provided a conduit for exploration and was perceived by Iraqi artists as a global space of shared humanity.

Various artist groups launched initiatives to convey the importance of national representation through culture, which included promoting the modern art movement in Iraq. This period set the stage for Iraq’s so-called golden age of the 1950s: a time of maturation for a generation of artists pivotal in initiating rigorous standards of art theory and practice, thus charting new possibilities for future generations.
The experimental ethos of the group continues to resonate today beyond Baghdad to direct and connect contemporary Iraqi artists around the world to each other.

Featured artists include Faraj Abbo, Sadik Kwaish Alfraji, Himat Mohammad Ali, Rasoul Alwan, Suad al-Attar, Qahtan Awni, Dia al-Azzawi, Bogus Bablanian, Amar Dawod, Ghassan Ghaib, Faiq (Faeq) Hassan, Mohammed Ghani Hikmat, Jabra Ibrahim Jabra, Rand Abdul Jabbar, Fouad Jihad, Saadi Al Kaabi, Ardash Kakafian, Salma Khoury, Hanaa Malallah, Mahmoud Obaidi, Widad al-Orfali, Khalid al-Rahal, Kareem Risan, Miran al-Saadi, Mahmoud Sabri, Naziha Salim, Nizar (Nazar) Salim, Shakir Hassan Al Said, Delair Shaker, Jewad Selim, Lorna Selim, Walid Siti, Ismail Fattah (Al-Turk), Madiha Umar, Khalil al-Ward, and Nazar Yahya.

The exhibition’s curator Dr. Nada Shabout has published widely on modern and contemporary Arab and Iraqi art and has curated numerous exhibitions. She has joined NYU Abu Dhabi as a senior investigator at al Mawrid Arab Center for the Study of Art and as a visiting professor of art history. She is the founding president of the Association for Modern and Contemporary Art from the Arab World, Iran, and Turkey (AMCA) and founding director of the Modern Art Iraq Archive (MAIA).
The exhibition is on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027.

items.titel: Guadalupe Rosales’s Portable Archive of East LA
items.anriss: If someone had described Los Angeles youth culture in the late 1990s, they might have invoked towheaded surfers, Sunset Strip hair bands, Beverly Hills teens, and the graffiti-soaked clubs that harbored New Wave and punk. Thanks to …

absaetze.t: In two new books, the artist weaves her archive of photos, ephemera, and flyers into the story of ’90s Chicanx youth culture, tracing both a personal and collective coming-of-age.
November 3, 2026 — 6 min read

If someone had described Los Angeles youth culture in the late 1990s, they might have invoked towheaded surfers, Sunset Strip hair bands, Beverly Hills teens, and the graffiti-soaked clubs that harbored New Wave and punk. Thanks to Guadalupe Rosales, our view of that time is now much more expansive.

Since 2015, the Los Angeles artist has collected the stories of the city’s Chicanx and Latinx youth — in particular, women and girls — via a pair of wildly popular Instagram pages, @veteranas_and_rucas and @map_pointz, which have become a collective archive of pre-internet adolescent life in the ’80s and ’90s. Big hair. Lined lips. Body-hugging tanks and baggy jeans. Not to mention the party flyers bearing titles like “Bad Influence” and “Titty Juice,” with their irreverent promises of liberation.

Over the years, Rosales has displayed this ephemera in imaginative ways, often in architectonic environments that pulse with the energy of nocturnal gatherings. In her installation for In Minor Keys, the international exhibition at the 61st Venice Biennale, infinity mirrors edged with neon are embedded with artifacts and suspended on a steel structure evoking the form of a SoCal bungalow.

A new project, however, finds the artist presenting her archive in more intimate ways. East of the River: A Memoir of Los Angeles Girlhood, published this fall, assembles many of the photos, flyers, news clips, and testimonials that followers have sent her for more than a decade. To that, she adds her own photographs and experiences, relaying the poignant story of her Eastside upbringing and the ways in which revelry with friends offered a respite from troubles both at home and in the larger city: the 1992 uprising, growing anti-immigrant sentiment, and gang violence. The latter claimed the life of her beloved cousin, Ever Sánchez, who was killed at a party in 1996. “It took me years to forgive those who took his life,” she writes, “but eventually I was able to turn the grief into altars and memorials and storytelling.”

items.titel: New York Studio School revamp unearths long-forgotten murals
items.anriss: A renovation project at the historic building—the original home of the Whitney Museum of American Art—has uncovered works by Robert E. Locher and Cecily Brown

absaetze.t: Back in 1907, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney established her sculpture studio in a converted stable and hayloft on MacDougal Alley in the heart of Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The heiress and artist then proceeded to procure four neighbouring brownstones one by one, with the Lincoln Memorial sculptor Daniel Chester French being the last holdout.

The five buildings that now comprise 8 West 8th Street are some of the New York art world’s most storied. It was here that Whitney promoted US artists at a time when they were widely denigrated, and where she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931. After the museum relocated uptown, the nascent New York Studio School (NYSS) moved into the compound in 1967.

Over the past century Edward Hopper sketched, John Cage lectured and Philip Guston taught within these walls. Countless other greats practised, exhibited or, in the case of Marianne Faithfull, lived in what is now a National Historic Landmark. “This building has been the incubator for American art for 120 years,” says the artist Matthew Ritchie, sitting in a bare-bones conference room on a warm September afternoon. It has also been sorely in need of a makeover at least since he was a student here in the 1990s.
Leaks and hazards

When Ritchie was named the school’s director last year, the roof and studio skylights—coveted by students for their diffused natural light—leaked, the nearly century-old cloth-wrapped wiring had deteriorated dangerously and wheelchair access was extremely limited. His priority was renovation. The first phase—including doubling the public exhibition space and creating a new accessible lecture and performance hall in wood with stepped seating—is set to be completed this autumn, and phase two will begin in the spring.

Prior to Ritchie’s arrival, the school had obtained public grants for the necessary work, but they required matching funds and their expiration date was fast approaching. He quickly marshalled forces. The board agreed to donate the required money, he says, and the school tapped Matthew Baird of Baird Architects to helm the overhaul.

Ritchie and Baird’s history of collaboration dates back 17 years and across two other local institutions. In 2009, they teamed up to consider the effects of rising sea levels on the built environment as part of the interdisciplinary Rising Currents project at the Museum of Modern Art. Just a few years later, they put their theories into practice after Hurricane Sandy tore through the city, its storm surge flooding much of downtown. Ritchie was on the board of the beloved alternative art space The Kitchen when it enlisted Baird to rehabilitate its waterlogged lobby and black-box theatre.

The architect’s sensitive execution on that project—he preserved visual evidence of flood damage, for example—made him an obvious choice for the NYSS project, which presented a similar challenge. “You have this really cool building that’s got this patina of great artists that have moved through it,” Baird says. “How do you not erase that?”
Buried treasure

Thanks to Baird and Ritchie’s handle-with-care edict, the construction crew was on the lookout for treasures buried beneath layers of plasterboard. The artist Cecily Brown had told Ritchie that she painted her first mural on a school wall when she was a student in the 1990s but could not remember where. And the school archives held numerous photos of murals Whitney had commissioned from the artist Robert E. Locher for the original carriage house.

Sure enough, the crew uncovered the work of both artists within a 24-hour period. Brown’s piece—featuring disembodied penises, two of them appearing to kiss—is in the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor. To prevent it from potentially distracting from exhibitions, the design team installed a shallow cabinet in front of the mural.

Ritchie jokes that the set-up resembles a gabinetto segreto, or secret room, the most famous of which was a locked vault of erotic artefacts from Pompeii and Herculaneum. “Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural? And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery?” he says with a laugh. “It’s the perfect combination.”

Workers discovered the two Locher murals where a bathroom and a hallway leading to it will be built. Intended to be viewed in the candlelight of Whitney’s dining room, one is a glimmering green, the other a trompe l’oeil image of doric columns. Baird tweaked the layout but not the location of the restroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” Ritchie says.

A less fortuitous surprise: the beams beneath Robert Winthrop Chanler’s flame-motif fireplace in Whitney’s original second-floor studio were cracking, requiring emergency shoring up to stop the ceiling from collapse—together with the priceless fireplace. “This is the urgency of renovation,” Ritchie says. “You can wait too long, and then you lose it all.”
Super-tight deadlines

Because of the grant deadlines for the first phase of the project, Baird needed to work at warp speed, condensing three years of planning, permitting, bidding and execution into one. Owing to New York City’s complex building code, he approached the $2.2m renovation as “100 small projects” rather than gutting the 59,000 sq. ft building. The landmark-restoration specialist Jonathan Raible is overseeing the new roof.

In addition to enhancing the first floor’s public spaces, Baird rewired the building, renovated the wreck of a kitchen and improved accessibility by adding a wheelchair lift to the performance hall. “You can’t have a public programme if you don’t provide correct facilities for the public,” Ritchie says. “You’re not really welcoming them.”

Climbing the narrow staircases to the maze of studios where the school’s 27 full-time, in-person students work, Baird speaks enthusiastically about the second phase of renovations, which will include a student coffee bar. In keeping with his preservationist instincts, he plans to relamp with LED bulbs the elegant Fresnel recessed box lighting that Whitney installed for evenly washed walls, and he hopes to restore the system of baffles that modulated direct light in the studios as well as undertake other restoration while safeguarding the landmark’s character.

Ritchie already has his eye on another, likely longer-term fix for the school: free tuition. “That would require a very large endowment from extremely generous single or multiple donors,” he says, giving his best impression of a silver-tongued salesman, “which we’re eagerly awaiting with an entirely unique naming opportunity.”

items.titel: À Paris, une exposition raconte l’une des plus belles histoires d’amitié de l’art entre Louis Aragon et Alékos Fassianós

absaetze.t: « Fassianos, ô Fassianos ! Je me souviens des premiers jours, quand me commença la surprise, d’une nouvelle façon d’aimer… » L’un compte parmi les plus grands auteurs français du XXe siècle, l’autre est considéré dans son pays natal comme le « Picasso grec ». À Paris, une exposition gratuite retrace, jusqu’au 12 décembre, la belle histoire d’amitié qui s’est écrite en mots et en images entre le peintre Alekos Fassianós (1935–2022) et Louis Aragon (1897–1982), quelques années seulement avant la disparition de ce dernier.

À la fin des années 1970, le vieux poète, que la mort a séparé d’Elsa, vit toujours dans leur appartement du 56 rue de Varenne, peuplé d’œuvres d’art et de souvenirs du couple. C’est là qu’il fait la rencontre du jeune peintre, qui n’a pas encore acquis la reconnaissance dont il jouira par la suite. Formé à l’École des beaux-arts d’Athènes dans l’atelier de Yánnis Móralis, Fassianós s’est installé à Paris en 1967 pour fuir la dictature des colonels.
Une même fascination pour l’amour et la mythologie

Depuis, il mène une carrière à rebours des canons de son temps. À l’heure où la tendance est à l’abstraction, il défend une peinture figurative et solaire, imprégnée des mythes et des couleurs de la Méditerranée. Cet artiste prolifique ne se limite d’ailleurs pas à la peinture puisqu’il est aussi écrivain, céramiste, designer, scénographe et architecte.

De ce véritable coup de foudre amical naît une relation de profonde estime à laquelle prend également part le poète d’origine iranienne Hamid Fouladvind (né en 1947). Collectionneur des œuvres de Fassianós avant même leur rencontre, Aragon lui consacre un texte très personnel, « Images chantées », qui vient clore ses Écrits sur l’art moderne et donne son titre à l’exposition.

Orchestrée par la curatrice Marion Gardair et présentée en collaboration avec le musée Fassianós d’Athènes et la Maison Triolet-Aragon, celle-ci réunit une dizaine d’œuvres et de précieux documents d’archives – lettres, dessins… Autant de témoignages qui révèlent comment les univers de ces deux artistes, décidément faits pour se rencontrer, se répondent autour d’une fascination commune pour l’amour et, bien sûr, la mythologie.
Des toiles comme surgies d’un rêve

Au-delà de cette amitié fertile, qui a donné lieu à de remarquables collaborations autour de livres, l’exposition met en lumière l’œuvre de Fassianós. Si le peintre est une véritable icône dans son pays, où un musée lui est consacré à Athènes, il demeure beaucoup moins connu en France.

Dans ses tableaux, les dieux de l’Antiquité côtoient des silhouettes anonymes alanguies, d’improbables cyclistes ou de beaux jeunes éphèbes. Ses visions aux couleurs éblouissantes, parfois rehaussées d’or, semblent surgir d’un rêve où les paysages et les intérieurs méditerranéens fusionnent avec l’urbanisme fonctionnel de la place d’Italie, aux abords de laquelle l’artiste avait installé son atelier. Un rêve éveillé où l’art et la poésie apparaissent comme l’un des plus beaux ciments de l’amitié.
